projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harold Spears was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: These photographs that I'm pointing to are photographs taken by the NYD militia personnel of the time when we were asked to, or ordered to go into an area that the Japanese held the island surrounded. But a thunderbolt has been shot down and crashed in the area there, and the Philippines guerillas had control of the immediate area there. So when we went in, the pilot had been taken off the plane by the friendly guerillas. These are photographs of the guerillas and their families that came down to the beach to meet us. We went through a narrow passage which we had no chart to determine its depth, or whether there was any town at all. Our medical doctor took the pilot off the plane and brought him aboard, and then we destroyed the plane, so the Japs couldn't use it later or take it out of the water and study it. The PBY came in a picked the pilot up and took him back to the hospital.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Were you in any of those pictures?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Well, I'm a Naval Officer and I'm aboard the ship, and these are the Marines coming up the beach.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Did you enlist in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: I did, I was in Duke Law School in the Fall of 1941, my first year of law school. On the first Sunday after Pearl Harbor, we went down to Raleigh from Durham to enlist, but they had not adjusted the physical standard to the point that they needed to in order to get those people. For example, they said I was flatfooted, stuff like that, and so I joined the Navy the first week of 1942, I think it was.

Of course it was a while before they could send me to Midshipman School, because they didn't have their Midshipman School set up yet. So there was a period of time after I enlisted before I went on active duty, but I went on active duty on October of 1942. I was in New York, Columbia University Midshipman's School, got my Hansen's (?) Commission in February 1943, was sent to Miami, Florida to have additional training in the, what they call the [illegible] SCTC Training Center, because our ship was primarily an anti-submarine escort ship in the North Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: What did you pick the branch of the Navy?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: At the time I graduated from High School, I really wanted to go to Annapolis, I didn't have my parental cooperation, and therefore I didn't go. When the draft was put in I was 1A, and I talked to the Draft Chairman I would have probably would have been called during the Fall Semester maybe which was my first year of Law School. But I went down anyway, because I told the Chairman of Draft Committee, "You're not going to draft me, if there is war, I'm going to join.'' Which I did. I'd say at that time, young people were not hesitate about joining, other than those who were objectors, ones who had reasons otherwise not to go, generally speaking, I was quite anxious to go.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: You never thought about the Air Force or the Army, did you?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: That is a funny story, too because actually when I was at Raleigh, the week after Pearl Harbor, they told me that I was color blind. That was the reason, they told me, that I couldn't get into the Navy at that particular point. When I went down to Norfolk to join the Navy, I thought, "Well, I would just join the Air Force and be a bombardier," because at that time they had said that if you are color blind then you wouldn't distinguish the camouflage colors and you wouldn't be fooled by the camouflage, so you would be an ideal bombardier. That's what I was told.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: What were you first days like, in the service?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: The first days, as apprentice seaman when you go into midshipman school you are in apprentice seaman. Very regimented, I had no trouble whatsoever with that because I had always been the person who had no difficulty in putting things were they belong. The rules were so strict that you had to put each book in a certain order on the shelf. If you put your navigation book where your seaman ship book should be, you got a demerit. In the closet, if you hung your raincoat out of place, you got a demerit. You had to put everything in order, you had to make you bunk or your bed, as they always said, you could throw a dime on it and it would bounce, and if you didn't do that right, you got a demerit. I had no trouble with any of that; I went right through without any difficulty. The academic part of the training was also relative easy for me, because I felt I had a very good education at both Marshall and Ironton High. My Math background was solid and it was necessary to have a good math background to do navigation. I never was a great swimmer because when I was a Md you couldn't swimmer anyplace except the Ohio River and it was too dirty, so I didn't do much swimming. So I had to pass the swimming test and we went to the Columbia University pool, which was a long pool to qualify for Olympic swimmers. I had to swim it a certain number of times and of course one of the problems a swimmer has is the breathing, if you get out of timing you could suck up a lot of water and you could chock. That would require swimming lessons which would be extra time and New York in the winter, etc. I got in the water and passed that test, I think when I passed that test that was the biggest hurdle.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: What you your job or assignment?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: I started out when the ship was in commission, incidentally I was a plank owner which means I was assigned to the USS Bull at the time of its commission and I served during the whole war on that same ship. At the time I was assigned to that ship, my assignment was the Assistant Battery Officer and Torpedo Officer. Later on I became the Gunner? Officer and just after the ending of hostility's I became Executive Officer which was second in command on the ship. Verelene; You saw a lot of combat; did you have any injuries from combat?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: No, I never had any injuries.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: In your unit was there much casualties?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Being aboard a ship like the destroyer escort is a lot like being in an airplane, if you're hit you are pretty much going to sink. If you're not hit then you don't have many casualties. We only had one causality that was assigned to us by the underwater demolition team, who was a young man from [illegible] Tennessee, who was a [illegible] I become quite well acquainted with and there's an old story that I don't need to go into, but he was killed at Iwo Jima when he was struck by a Howitzer off the beach. That was a tough one.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Did you get a lot of phone calls and letters from home when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: I didn't get any phone calls; they didn't know where I was. I will tell you another funny story that will go with that. There was another Harold Spears that lived here in Pedro, Ohio. I guess we were distantly related but weren't acquainted because we just didn't get around much in those days. Anyways, he became a Green Corp fighter pilot. As a matter of fact, he became an Ace. At one point in the Pacific during all these battles, we received the newspapers, when we were able to get the mail which was once about every two or three weeks, maybe every month, along with them would be the newspapers. One day when I picked up the Ironton paper I saw the headline, 'HAROLD SPEARS KILLED", that was a shock to read that in the paper, of course it was the other Harold Spears.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Of course we were in the Officers room and I can't complain about the food. The problem we had was the fact that we didn't get fresh vegetables, food and milk. When the time came that you were able to get fresh food, you ate it like it was going out of style. That was true even in the North Atlantic because we would go over on a convoy, and it would be gone in a month. During that little period of time we wouldn't have any greenery like a salad, or we wouldn't have fresh milk. I remember when we would come into New York or Boston about the first place we could run to was a restaurant where we could stock up on things like that.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: How did you entertain yourselves on that ship?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Well, there wasn't any entertainment on the ship, but when we went into port there was the Officer's Club. And we would generally go to the Officer's Club. Eddie Duchin, who you probably don't know anything about, was assigned to one of our ships in our division. When we would go to Northern Ireland to the Officer's Club, Eddie would be there and play the piano. He was a tremendous piano player; he could play any tune that you could imagine, so we had a lot of fun with him.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: What did you do during your leaves?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: The only leave that I had was when I graduated from midshipman school; I got to come home for a week. During that time, our ship was being converted in August 1944; in July 19441 had a leave to come home for a week. That was the only leaves that I remember, because I was on sea duty the whole time. Two leaves in thee and half years.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: What place outside of the US did you go?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Our European base was Londonderry and Belfast, Ireland. We had made trips to Dutch West Indies convoy, the Island there, Crusoe or something like that. It is in the Dutch West Indies and of course we went through the Panama Canal and we went over to the West Coast and to Pearl Harbor and Ulithe and the Philippine Islands, Siapan, etc., we got around.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Do you recall any humorous events?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: I can remember one time when we were in Londonderry which was in February 1944, the weather forecast was for severe weather around home, and there also was a German wolf pack waiting for our convoy. We had an Officer aboard who was Catholic and he saw me on the ship before we were employed to leave. He said, "Harold, I had not been to church for a long time, and I need someone to go with me, would you go?" I said, "Frank, you are Catholic and I am Protestant, and I know from experience that if I went to a Catholic church you're going to be on your knees and I will be standing up when I should be down. And when you come up, I will be down and it's going to be embarrassing. I don't think I'd better go." "Oh!" he said, "You have got to go with me, cos I really feel like I have to go." I said, "Frank, I don't feel like I should go." He said, "111 make you a deal, if you go with me well both stand up in the back of the church and pretend like we are both Protestants." And we did.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Did you ever pull any pranks on anybody or have any pranks pulled on you?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Well, there wasn't a whole lot of joking going on. I don't recall anything like that. They were afraid of me because I was a Regulation kind of Officer and I enforced the rules. We used to sing, you weren't allowed to drink on the ship. We have a reunion every year from our ship; I just got back from Albany, NY. There is evidence of badges where I've been to the reunion every year for a long time; fewer and fewer people are showing up. We are down to about 30 that show up, including wives. This many years later we don't have the differences between Officers and men the way we used to, but there is still a bit of separation. Of course in the Navy, stuffs much like it is in the Army and even the Air Force. In the Navy there's kind of a separation between the enlisted personnel and the Officer's, and even though I've known these fellows for, we've had reunions for over ten years, get to know them quite well, I am still Mr. Spears, I am not Hal. I enjoy going to these reunions because they all are very respectful and they are very nice and they are good friends. I am still their superior, I am still an Officer. We had a reunion a few years ago; I overheard some of the men saying, "Those are the fellas that brought us home safely."

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Where were you when your service ended?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: I was in Manila, which was after the war. I was in the service until Jan 1946 because of the fact there were certain points that people received, most of the men that were married got more points than those who were single and I was single. I was still assigned to duty in Jan 1946 and we were in Manila, I was Executive Officer at that time and the Captain and I agreed that we would leave the ship together, and we did. We were able to get a replacement for the Captain and there was someone who was qualified to take my place and so we left the ship together at Manila and I came back to San Francisco. I was offered an extra half strip, they said if I would stay in they would promote me to Lt. Commander, but you will have to take command of the ship. Well at that time the experienced ranks and the Experience Officers were being discharged. The ships who were out in the Philippines and ports of that nature were receiving people who had no experience at sea so there were accidents happening, ships were not being handled properly, some were going [illegible]. Of course Captains were responsible for all these things, I just felt like a six month tour of duty, it wasn't worth going into all that.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Do you remember the day Pearl Harbor was bombed, where were you?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: I sure do, I was at Duke Law School in the stacks at the library, preparing a document for what they call the Family Purpose Doctrine in Ohio. I remember it was along 2:00 in the afternoon, there was some commotion and some excitement on the steps on the Law School, which was above the library stacks where I was sitting. I went out to see what it was about and learned about Pearl Harbor, everyone knew their lives where about to be changed. There was some in the Reserves who expected to be called right away. I remember one fella who I knew quite well, who was in my class, his father was an Army Captain who was in the Philippine Island and this young man was really disturbed as you might well expect. I don't know whether he ever did learn his father's fate, and I never saw him after that. I can remember his name was Keltner and he was from Texas and I don't know what happened.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: When you came back home after your discharge, did you go back to school?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Yes, back to Duke Law School, I had two more years to complete. I had the GI Bill, which helped a lot.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Oh yea, especially among the Officer personnel. We were quite close, you just don't go through the things we went through without getting close. Verlene: Do you ever see any other them lately?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Well, yes, course those who are still around and come to these reunions, not too many come. The Captain of our ship, one of the Captains, was the fella who was the Gunnery Officers when I was Assistant Gunnery Officer. He later became Executive and then Captain. He was a Lawyer in Washington, DC and he and I have been particularly close, because when we were in Florida at the sub chaser (?) training station he and his wife were there, of course I was single. But I can remember when we were ordered from Miami, Florida to Norfolk where we were training our nucleus crew, we rode the train from Miami to Norfolk and they had a new little girl, just a baby. I never knew anything about babies, but we were in the train, and they wanted to go back to the diner to have dinner and I agreed to hold the baby for them and I was scared to death.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: We know what kind of career you had after the war, you have been a Judge and..

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Yes, I was Prosecutor for eight years, then I became a Judge, then went back into practice.

sp.speaker: Verlene Anderson
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we haven't covered in the interview?

sp.speaker: Harold Spears
sp.p: Well, I think one of the things I will never forget is the Hurricane in the North Atlantic in February of 1944. We were coming back from Ireland, it was the same trip I referred to awhile ago when my friend wanted to go to church, and we got involved in an Hurricane. The waves were higher than the main mast of our ship, which means they were every bit of seventy five feet. Now if you can imagine waves seventy five feet high, and the Hurricane lasted two or three days, and during that whole period of time, course I was an Officer of the deck, which means for four hours I was in charge of the bridge and in charge of the ship. Four hours on and eight hours off. During that whole period of time, the Destroyer Escort was 306 feet long and the main mast was about 72 feet high, and so when we go over the top of the crest part of the waves, the screws and the propeller would go out in the water. We would have no control, the ship would start down in the trough and we would have to fight it to get it straight, if it went down sideways it would roll over and we would sink. We had to fight to keep that ship in the sea and as soon as the screws and rudder got in the water, and if it was headed for the port side, we would have to go full rudder and all ahead flake on the port engine to straighten it out. We fought that thing for two or three days, that was a scary thing. We had a fire during that time, aboard that time, because the sea water was blowing horizontally. The sea water blew inside the vents and set a generator on fire, the repair parties were able to get the fire under control, if we had lost power, we would have sunk. There were [illegible] in that room, he came back into New York, following that Hurricane, the gun shield on the bow, which is steel circular gun shell that surrounds the guns, was mashed flat. Just like a giant had stepped on it, the [illegible] bow had a dent in it, a huge dent bending the skin of the ship, and the whole ship was pushed in there where it has been hit by the sea. The main mast was wobbling back and forth, the boat and the [illegible] was loose. It took two weeks to put the ship back together because of the damage that Hurricane had done. Incidentally, when the Destroyer escort was produced it was considered to be expendable, and we were told the Navy would be glad to trade a submarine u-boat for a Destroyer escort. So if we encountered a submarine our first maneuver was to ram, because they figured they didn't know for sure if these DEs could withstand the rigors of the heavy seas of the North Atlantic, we were plainly told we were expendable. Of course, the DE turned out the DE was much more rugged than they had thought it would be. When we were trying to go through that Hurricane the bunks we had would be chained to the overhead in order to get any sleep at all, you would have to take up three, four or five chain links so that instead of your bunks being flat, it would be at an angle and you could slip down in the crack so you wouldn't roll out when the ship rolled. When you got ready to eat, there was no way you could eat, except the chairs were latched to pad eyes which was attached to the deck, and you latched these chairs to these pad eyes so it wouldn't slide back and forth and you would take your dinner and let it rock back and forth and you neat it as the ship rolled. You couldn't set a glass down; you would have to have your glass... I remember having Thanksgiving dinner on the bridge one time, in a very heavy sea. I was on watch, they had a pretty bad dinner, prepared, it was a dark, grey, North Atlantic. Of course it was very little activity because the sea was too rough to put on our U-Boats, all we had to do was keep stationed.
